text.p: This is how major world bond markets were trading in late European business on Monday.

GERMANY - Bund futures ended holiday-shortened DTB trading session with mild gains. The March Bund future on the London International Financial Futures and Options Exchange (LIFFE) was trading at 100.80, up 0.13 from Friday's settlement price.

BRITAIN - UK gilts dipped in late trade, losing ground to Bunds which held on to a small part of the day's gains. The March long gilt future on LIFFE was trading at 109-30/32, down 03/32 from Friday's settlement price.

FRANCE - French bond and PIBOR futures closed unchanged, ending a very quiet session without strong impulse in either direction. The March notional bond future on the MATIF in Paris settled at 129.30 unchanged from Friday's settlement price.

ITALY - The Italian cash bond market staggered over the finishing line with mild gains in the penultimate trading session of the year while futures skated to the finish some 30 basis points ahead. The March bond future on LIFFE was trading at 128.55 up 0.30 from Friday's settlement price.

UNITED STATES - U.S. Treasury prices remained tightly range bound at midday on Monday as economic data releases failed to shake the market out of its torpor. The March Treasury bond future on the Chicago Board of Trade was trading at 114-03/32, up 05/32 from Friday's settlement price. The long bond was quoted to yield 6.52 percent.

JAPAN - Cash and futures JGBs ended the last trading session for the year on Monday with mild losses due mainly to hedge selling by institutional investors, traders said. In after hours trading the March future on LIFFE was trading at 124.29, up 0.08 from Friday's settlement price on the Tokyo Stock Exchange.
EUROBONDS - A short-dated yen bond was the only Eurobond offering on Monday, with most players on holiday.

Mitsubishi Corp Finance issued a 50 billion yen July 1998 bond which paid a 1.5 percent coupon and was issued at 101.74. Lead manager Daiwa was unavailable for comment. Little issuance was expected this week, but bankers would start to draw up plans for the usual January rush once investors came back to their desks on January 2. "There is little firm information available now, but once investors return on Thursday things will get into gear," said a syndicate manager at a European bank.
